You use adjectives and nouns with a fixed preposition: Ich bin stolz auf dich. Sie ist gespannt auf das Konzert. Er hat Angst vor dem Auftritt. — and you replace things with darauf, davor, dafür.

Learn adjectives with a fixed preposition together with the preposition and the case.
Learn nouns with a preposition (often the same as the verb: sich freuen auf → die Vorfreude auf).
Replace the object with da(r)- (stolz darauf) or with preposition + pronoun for people (stolz auf sie).
Ask questions with wo(r)- (Worauf bist du gespannt?) or preposition + wen/wem (Auf wen bist du stolz?).
Announce a clause with da(r)- (Ich bin stolz darauf, dass…).

It's September 2034. With the donations from Mara's wedding, the Pankow music school has created the “Friedrich Mertens” scholarship. The first scholarship holder is Elif. Tomorrow she has her first concert at the music school. Grete listens to her for the last time at the care home.
Elif, child. Are you looking forward to tomorrow?
I'm scared. Really scared. What do I do if I forget everything? Like Mum back then?
Then you listen to the metronome. Stage fright is normal. I was afraid before every concert, for seventy years. Anyone who isn't afraid isn't interested in the music, only in themselves.
Are you satisfied with the second part? I still play it too fast.
I'm never completely satisfied. That's my job. But I'm proud of you. Very proud. And Friedrich would have been too.
I'm so grateful for the scholarship. And for you. Without you I would never have started.
Nonsense. You already took joy in the piano before you met me. I just made sure you didn't lose that joy.
Mrs Hoffmann, are you coming tomorrow? Please. I'm only not nervous if you're sitting in the front row.
Child, I'm ninety-eight. I depend on a wheelchair and on Mara, who pushes me. But yes. I'm coming. You can count on that.
And what if I make a mistake?
Then you keep playing. The audience isn't curious to hear your mistakes. They're curious to hear you.
Like verbs (chapter 62), many adjectives have a fixed preposition. You learn them in pairs:
Ich bin gespannt auf das Konzert.
Danke, ich bin dankbar für deine Hilfe.
Bist du zufrieden mit dem Ergebnis?
Wir sind begeistert von der Idee.
Sie ist besorgt um ihren Vater.
Ich bin nervös vor der Prüfung.
“gespannt auf” doesn't mean “tense”, but “curious / eager to find out”: “Ich bin gespannt, wie es weitergeht” = I can't wait to see how it goes on.
Sie hat Angst vor dem Auftritt.
Er hat großes Interesse an Geschichte.
Ich habe Lust auf ein Eis.
Ich habe eine Bitte um Hilfe.
Ihr Stolz auf die Tochter war groß.
The noun often keeps the preposition of the verb or adjective: sich interessieren für / interessiert an / das Interesse an (careful: the verb takes “für”, the adjective and the noun take “an”!).
The same rules as for verbs with a preposition:
Ich bin stolz darauf. (auf das Konzert)
Ich bin stolz auf sie. (auf Elif)
With a clause: “Ich bin stolz darauf, dass du nie aufgegeben hast.” / “Ich habe Lust darauf, heute Abend zu tanzen.”

English “of”, “in” or “on” correspond to many different German prepositions (proud of = stolz auf, afraid of = Angst vor, dependent on = abhängig von). Don't translate the preposition, learn the pair.
Are you satisfied with the result?
She is very interested in music.
I'm not in the mood for scales.
I can't wait to see how it goes on.
I'm afraid of what comes next.
I'm proud that you never gave up.
Wie lange hatte Grete vor Konzerten Angst?
von einem Rollstuhl und von Mara

The idea for the scholarship had come from Mara, like so many ideas that year. The wedding guests had donated money instead of gifts, for the benefit of the Pankow music school, and in the end it came to more than four thousand euros. On top of that came the donations from Friedrich's memorial service and an anonymous transfer of a thousand euros, which the whole of Kastanienallee knew came from Katrin Krüger, although she never admitted it. The music school was enthusiastic about the idea. It set up the “Friedrich Mertens Scholarship” for a child who wanted to learn the piano and couldn't afford it. The jury was made up of three teachers from the music school and an honorary jury member, who sat in a wheelchair in the front row and tapped out the beat with a pencil on her knee for every child who played.

Elif hadn't wanted to play at the audition. She had said it was unfair, because she knew Mrs Hoffmann, and Mrs Hoffmann was on the jury. Grete had looked at her with her clearest, most ironic look and said: “Child, in seventy years I have never favoured a child I know. I have always judged them more strictly. Ask your mother.” Ayşe had nodded. And so in June Elif had played at the audition, together with eleven other children, and Grete had listened to her longer and more strictly than to all the others, and at the end she was the only one on the jury who said she wasn't completely satisfied with the second part. The other three jury members had voted for Elif. Grete had abstained. “On principle,” she said later. But Mara, who was pushing her home, saw that she smiled all the way.

Elif had practised all summer. Two hours every day at the black piano in the Yilmaz family's living room, on the second floor of number thirty-three, with the window open, so that half of Kastanienallee was listening. The neighbours didn't complain. Quite the opposite. Mrs Schulze from the ground floor, who was ninety-one by now, put a chair out in the courtyard every afternoon at four and listened, with a cup of coffee and her eyes closed. And Michael Kühn, the owner of the building, who came to visit from Munich in July, sat on the stairs for half an hour and listened, and then said it was the most beautiful thing that had ever happened in this building since Mrs Brandt had read «Emil and the Detectives» with him.

The scholarship holder's concert took place on the last Sunday in September, in the small hall of the Pankow music school, an old building from the late nineteenth century with stucco on the ceiling and a grand piano almost as old as Grete. The hall had eighty seats. A hundred and twenty people came. Half of Kastanienallee, the whole Yilmaz family with uncles and aunts from Neukölln and Kreuzberg, Elif's class with Jakob as their teacher, the residents of the “Am Kollwitzpark” care home in a minibus, Mr Petrowski from room 14 in a suit nobody had seen him in for ten years. People stood along the walls and in the doorway. The caretaker of the music school said this broke the fire safety regulations. Then he sat down on the stairs and listened.

Grete sat in the front row, in her wheelchair, in black, with her pearl necklace, and next to her Mara, five months pregnant, with one hand on her belly. Beside them Ludwig, with the brass bell in his jacket pocket, which he had promised not to use. Ayşe and her husband sat behind them, so nervous that Mr Yilmaz, the quiet bus driver, kept twisting his cap in his hands until it lost its shape. “I'm more nervous than at my own wedding,” he whispered to Ludwig. Ludwig nodded. “That's normal,” he whispered back. “You're always prouder of your own children than of yourself. And more afraid for them.”

Shortly before the concert, Elif had come to Grete once more, backstage, in a small room with an old piano and a mirror. She was pale and trembling. “I don't feel like it any more,” she had said. “I want to go home.” Grete hadn't said anything. She had just pointed to the small piano, and Elif had sat down and played a scale, then another, and another, slowly, and after the fifth scale she had stopped trembling. “You see,” Grete had said. “Stage fright is like a barking dog. If you give it scales, it lies down.”

Then Elif came in. She was wearing a navy dress her mother had sewn, her hair was braided into a plait, and under her arm she wasn't carrying sheet music but something small, made of wood. She went to the piano, bowed, exactly as deeply as Grete had taught her, and placed the old metronome on the piano. Mr Wendland's metronome, from the cellar in 1943. She didn't set its pendulum going. She just put it there, so that it would be there. Then she sat down, glanced once briefly at the front row, at Grete, and began.
Outside, beyond the tall windows, the sun was setting, and the last light fell red on the old piano.

She played Schumann, two pieces from “Scenes from Childhood”, then a little Haydn sonata, and at the end a piece that nobody could find in the programme, because it wasn't in the programme. It was a simple piece, a melody like a children's song, with a turn in the middle that sounded sad and then didn't any more. Ludwig recognised it after three bars. It was Mirko's song. The song “For S.”, which a fifteen-year-old boy had written in 1989 on a bad guitar for a girl with pigtails. Mirko had arranged it for piano and given it to Elif in the summer. And in the fourth row sat Susanne, who had come from Hanover, with her hand over her mouth.

Elif made a mistake. Just once, in the second part of the Haydn sonata, exactly in the passage Grete had never been satisfied with. She played too fast, hit a wrong note and stopped for a second. A hundred and twenty people held their breath. Ayşe grabbed her husband's hand. And Elif looked at the metronome standing calmly on the piano, not ticking, took a breath and played on. More slowly. Exactly as slowly as Grete had been asking her to for a year. And suddenly the passage sounded different. Warmer. As if the mistake had reminded her of something she had almost forgotten.

When she had finished, the hall was silent. Elif stood up, bowed, and then, before anyone could applaud, a quiet, hoarse voice was heard from the front row. Grete had raised herself up in her wheelchair as far as she could. “The second part,” she said, loudly enough for the whole hall to hear. “After the mistake. That was right. At last.” And then she applauded. Alone. Slowly, with her thin old hands that had played the piano for ninety years. And then everyone applauded, a hundred and twenty people, and the caretaker on the stairs, and Mr Petrowski stood up and shouted “Bravo!”, and Ludwig couldn't hold back any longer and rang the brass bell, once, loud and clear, even though he had promised.

After the concert, Elif came over to Grete, knelt beside the wheelchair and asked quietly: “Were you satisfied?” Grete looked at her for a long time. Then she took Elif's hand. “Child,” she said. “I have never in my life been completely satisfied. Neither with myself nor with my pupils. That's my job. But today I'm something else. Today I'm proud. And grateful. Because I've lived long enough to hear this.” Elif hugged her, carefully, because of the wheelchair and the pearl necklace, and Grete let her, which she rarely did, and the music school's photographer took a photo that later hung next to Friedrich's photo in the common room of the care home, with the caption: “The first scholarship holder and her teacher. September 2034.”

In the evening there was a small celebration at the café “Bei Ingrid”. Lena had baked a cake in the shape of a piano, with black and white chocolate keys, and Elif was allowed to be the first to press the brass bell by the till, even though she hadn't ordered cocoa. Mr Yilmaz gave a speech, his first in Germany, three sentences long, with red ears. He said he had come from Kayseri as a young man to drive buses and had never thought that one day his daughter would play in a concert hall. “I am grateful for this country,” he said. “And for this street. And for Mrs Hoffmann.” Then he quickly sat down again, everyone applauded, and Ayşe gave him a kiss on the cheek, in front of everyone, which she had never done in twenty years of marriage.

Grete hadn't come to the celebration at the café. She was tired, she had said, and Mara had taken her back to the care home. But when Mara looked in on her late in the evening to see how she was, Grete wasn't in bed, but in the armchair by the window, with Friedrich's photograph on her knees, the photograph from the Konzerthaus in 1960. She was talking quietly to him. Mara stayed in the doorway and heard a single sentence before she quietly left: “She played the second part right, Friedrich. After the mistake. Exactly the way I should have played it for you in 1960.”
